title: Component interpolation under leading Hilbert weight inequalities
statement:
Let $k$ be algebraically closed, $g\ge2$, $d>9(g-1)$ and $r=d+1-g$. Let $D\subset\mathbf P^{r-1}_k$ be a connected reduced nodal curve, with node model $k[[u,v]]/(uv)$ [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion, def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series], Hilbert polynomial $dm+1-g$, and complete nondegenerate hyperplane embedding $L=\mathcal O_D(1)$, with $h^0(D,L)=r$ and $H^1(D,L)=0$. Assume that every weighted flag of linear forms with integral weights in $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ satisfies
$$a_F\le\frac d r\sum_iw_i,$$
where the leading coefficient $a_F$ is defined by [lem-sfb-bounded-hilbert-weight-polynomials]. For any reduced union $Y$ of components and any component $E$ of the normalization of its reduced complement, let $b_E$ count the preimages on $E$ of nodes joining that component to $Y$. Then either
$$\deg_E L\ge b_E,$$
or $E$ maps isomorphically to a rational normal component and $\deg_E L=b_E-1$. A rational normal curve of degree $e$ means a smooth rational curve whose embedding in its own linear span is the complete degree-$e$ embedding of $\mathbf P^1$. Component degrees below are degrees of the pulled-back hyperplane line on the smooth normalized components [def-sc-normalization, def-pc-degree-line-bundle].

source.place: Section 3.2 proof of Theorem 8, step (9), printed p.14: component interpolation prerequisite before the subcurve inequality. Agent leading-weight formulation of that step (the span flags used have weights zero and one). Local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Write $T_i$ for the reduced irreducible components of $D$, and $e_i=\deg_{\widetilde T_i}L$. Projectivity gives properness by [lem-pc-projective-proper], and finite type over the Noetherian field gives Noetherianity by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian]. There are finitely many components, with finite smooth proper connected normalizations, by [lem-trf-reduced-curve-normalization-genus]. For every union $A$ of components, [lem-trf-nodal-subcurve-boundary] identifies its boundary with its reduced complement as finitely many distinct $k$-points, each smooth on both sides, and says $A$ is nodal. Let $k_A$ be this number and $e_A=\sum_{T_i\subset A}e_i$. The hyperplane line is ample: its coordinate sections have affine nonvanishing opens, the intersections of $D$ with the standard affine charts, as in [def-weil-pbc-ample-invertible-module]. Thus [lem-trf-fibre-degree-ample-criterion] gives $e_i\ge1$.

source.place: Tag 0B5Y, lemma-ampleness-in-terms-of-degrees-components; normalization and nodal-boundary tools cited in the step

proof.text: Every reduced union $A$ is nonspecial for $L|_A$. Indeed for its closed immersion $i:A\hookrightarrow D$, [lem-pc-closed-immersion-coherent-cohomology] says $i_*(L|_A)$ is coherent and computes its cohomology on $D$. The restriction $L\twoheadrightarrow i_*(L|_A)$ is surjective in local line-bundle trivializations. Its kernel $K$ is coherent by [lem-weil-pbc-coherent-kernel-cokernel-locnoeth]. Now [lem-sc-noetherian-cohomology-above-dimension] gives $H^2(D,K)=0$, and the long exact sequence of [pqf-def-cohomology], together with the assumed $H^1(D,L)=0$, gives $H^1(A,L|_A)=0$. The same dimension-vanishing statement gives $H^j(A,L|_A)=0$ for $j\ge2$. Cohomology is finite-dimensional by [lem-pc-coherent-hi], since $A$ is proper over the field. Consequently $h^0(A,L|_A)=\chi(A,L|_A)$. This includes disconnected unions; for the empty union both sides are zero.

source.place: Tags 01Y0, lemma-coherent-abelian-Noetherian; 089W, lemma-relative-affine-cohomology; cohomology.tex Tag 02UZ, proposition-vanishing-Noetherian

proof.text:
Apply [lem-trf-nodal-normalization-quotient] to each connected component of $A$, and tensor its exact sequence by $L|_A$. Tensoring by a line is exact, since locally it is tensoring by a free module of rank one. In the middle term, local trivializations identify $(
u_*\mathcal O_{\widetilde A})\otimes L$ with $
u_*
u^*L$. The last term $Q$ has zero-dimensional support and unchanged Euler characteristic after tensoring by [lem-pc-chi-zero-dim-support]. Euler additivity [lem-pc-euler-additive], the affine cohomology comparison for the finite normalization [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-cohomology-edge], and the degree definition [def-pc-degree-line-bundle] therefore give
$$\chi(A,L|_A)-\chi(A,\mathcal O_A)=\sum_{T_i\subset A} igl(\chi(\widetilde T_i,
u_i^*L)-\chi(\widetilde T_i,\mathcal O) igr)=e_A.$$
Thus $h^0(A,L|_A)=e_A+\chi(A,\mathcal O_A)$ by step 2. The same computation for a single $T_i$ also identifies its intrinsic degree with $e_i$.

source.place: Tags 0C1R, lemma-prepare-delta-invariant; 0AYT, lemma-chi-tensor-finite; curves.tex Tag 0CBW, lemma-split-node

proof.text:
For an irreducible component $T$, put $p_T=\dim_kH^1(T,\mathcal O_T)\ge0$. By [lem-sc-global-functions], $h^0(T,\mathcal O_T)=1$, and higher cohomology vanishes by [lem-sc-noetherian-cohomology-above-dimension]. Hence $\chi(T,\mathcal O_T)=1-p_T$. If $T$ is outside a union $A$ and meets $A$ in $\ell$ nodes, the formula of [lem-trf-nodal-curve-normalization-euler], summed over connected components, gives
$$\chi(A\cup T,\mathcal O)=\chi(A,\mathcal O_A)+1-p_T-\ell.$$
In fact the component count adds, the normalized genera add, and the internal-node count adds with $\ell$ additional nodes; self-nodes were already counted inside $T$. Step 3 consequently gives
$$h^0(A\cup T,L)-h^0(A,L)=e_T+1-p_T-\ell.$$
If $u$ counts nodes from $T$ to the components outside $A\cup T$, counting the three kinds of boundary edges gives $k_{A\cup T}-k_A=u-\ell$.

source.place: Nodal normalization Euler formula, Tag 0CBW; elementary component and edge counts

proof.text:
Put $h=g-1>0$, $\epsilon=h/d\in(0,1/9)$ and $q=r/d=1-\epsilon>8/9$. Define for each reduced union
$$\Delta(A)=h^0(A,L|_A)-q(e_A+k_A/2).$$
The Hilbert-polynomial comparison [lem-sfb-projective-hilbert-polynomial-dimension] gives $\chi(D,\mathcal O_D(m))=dm+1-g$ at every integer $m$. Taking $m=1$ and $m=0$ and using step 3 yields $e_D=d$. Therefore $\Delta(D)=r-qd=0$, and $\Delta(\varnothing)=0$. Suppose some $\Delta(A)<0$, and choose such an $A$ maximal under inclusion among the finitely many unions. Then $A$ is nonempty and proper, and $\Delta(A\cup T)\ge0$ for every component $T$ outside $A$.

source.place: After Proposition 1.0.9, printed pp.64--65: maximal subcurve violating the subcurve inequality; leading-weight version reconstructed by NZ

proof.text: If each normalized component of the complement of this $A$ has degree at least its number of boundary branches to $A$, apply [lem-sfb-subcurve-span-weight-bound] with every boundary branch chosen and $X=D$. Its first alternative holds on every component, so its rational-normal exception is not being assumed. It gives a zero/one flag with quotient dimension $s\le h^0(A,L|_A)$ and $a_F\ge e_A+k_A/2$. The hypothesis of the item applies to this flag since $\{0,1\}\subset\{0,1,2,3,4\}$. It gives $a_F\le(d/r)s=s/q$, and thus $\Delta(A)\ge0$, a contradiction. Therefore some component $T$ outside $A$ has $e=e_T<\ell$, where $\ell$ counts its nodes joining $A$. These nodes are distinct smooth points on $T$, so their number agrees with the number of their preimages on its normalization. In particular $\ell\ge e+1\ge2$.

source.place: Proposition 1.0.7, printed pp.55--61, only the degree-bounded boundary case; maximal-subcurve argument on pp.64--65

proof.text:
For this $T$ let $u\ge0$ and $p=p_T\ge0$ be as in step 4. Maximality and $\Delta(A)<0$ give $\Delta(A\cup T)-\Delta(A)>0$. On the other hand step 4 computes this difference as
$$\epsilon e+1-p-(1-q/2)\ell-qu/2.$$
Since $e\le\ell-1$ and $\epsilon=1-q>0$, it is at most
$$\epsilon(\ell-1)+1-p-(1-q/2)\ell-qu/2
=q\bigl(1-(\ell+u)/2\bigr)-p\le0,$$
the last inequality using $\ell\ge2$. This contradicts strict positivity. Thus there is no violating union:
$$q(e_A+k_A/2)\le h^0(A,L|_A)\quad\text{for every reduced union }A.$$
The argument allowed disconnected $A$ throughout. It used only the degree-bounded case of the span estimate, so never assumed the component interpolation being proved.

source.place: Printed pp.64--65, maximal violating subcurve; explicit difference calculation, with no finite-m error

proof.text:
Now fix $Y$ and $E$ in the statement, and write $T$ for the irreducible component of $D$ whose normalization is $E$. Let $e=\deg_E L$, $b=b_E$, and let $\kappa=k_T$ count all nodes joining $T$ to other components of $D$. Since $T$ is outside $Y$, $0\le b\le\kappa$. If $e\ge b$ the first conclusion holds. Otherwise $b\ge e+1$, so $\kappa\ge e+1$. Step 7 with $A=T$, and steps 3--4, give
$$q(e+\kappa/2)\le h^0(T,L)=e+1-p_T.$$
Using $\kappa\ge e+1$ and $q=1-\epsilon$, this implies
$$(1-3\epsilon)e\le1+\epsilon-2p_T.$$
The left side is positive, so the integer $p_T\ge0$ is zero. If $e\ge2$, the left side is at least $2-6\epsilon>1+\epsilon$ because $\epsilon<1/9<1/7$, a contradiction. Therefore $e=1$. The same inequality before substituting $\kappa$ gives
$$\kappa\le2(1+\epsilon)/(1-\epsilon)<5/2.$$
Since $\kappa\ge b\ge2$ are integers, $\kappa=b=2$. Thus $e=b-1$.

source.place: Section 3.2 Theorem 8 proof step (9), printed p.14; component consequence of the explicitly derived subcurve inequality

proof.text: In the exceptional case $T$ is a proper integral curve, $H^0(T,\mathcal O_T)=k$ by step 4, $H^1(T,\mathcal O_T)=0$ since $p_T=0$, and $\deg_T(L|_T)=e=1$ by step 3. Hence [lem-trf-pointed-genus-zero-projective-line] gives $T\cong\mathbf P^1_k$. In particular $T$ is smooth. The normalization is an isomorphism over the smooth locus by [lem-trf-nodal-normalization-adjunction], so $E\to T$ is an isomorphism. Also step 3 gives $h^0(T,L|_T)=2$. Let $U$ be the image of ambient linear forms in this space. These coordinate sections generate $L|_T$ at every point. If $\dim U=1$, its generator is nowhere zero and trivializes $L|_T$, whose degree would then be $\chi(\mathcal O_T)-\chi(\mathcal O_T)=0$, contradicting degree one. Thus $\dim U=2$ and $U=H^0(T,L|_T)$. Its embedding in its own linear span is therefore the complete degree-one embedding of $\mathbf P^1$, exactly a rational normal component in the stated convention. With $e=b-1$ from step 8 this proves the second alternative. The cases $Y=\varnothing$ or no complementary component are already covered by $b=0$ or vacuity.
